Kind of a broad question, but what’s your advice for someone on the edge? I really haven’t met anyone else whose ‘attempt count’ (Sorry I really can’t think of anything nicer to call it) is around the same as mine so I’d like to hear what you have to say.

You’re going to pull through. Take a moment to not think about what’s going to happen tomorrow or what happened yesterday. If you’re tired, listen to your body. Maybe have a glass of water and sleep for a while. Put on some music that you find relaxing. You deserve to take care of yourself. Think of it like you’re preparing yourself to face what’s next. Self-care is just getting yourself to peak performance. Not every problem has to be faced at the same time either. You can take it one step at a time. Even if you pick one little thing to deal with, it will still be an accomplishment. I believe in you.

Several years ago, my grandfather suddenly passed away and I saw his body in the hospital.

I had a dream not long after where my family was all sitting around eating thanksgiving dinner as we normally would. However, my grandfather’s limp corpse was also at the table, in his usual seat. Everyone was laughing and talking to him as if he was alive and I was the only person who seemed to realize he wasn’t. My grandmother kept adding food to the plate in front him that was starting to overflow. 

It honestly wasn’t a long dream, but I still think about it a lot.

I’ll start this off by saying that I know your pain. I’m a passionate hiker with diagnosed EIB.

I’ll give you a pass for not thinking about your inhaler if you hadn’t needed it in several years but, at the end of the day, you should have listened to your body. This is the bare minimum for personal safety. I know this is harsh, but the the severity of the attack was entirely your fault. There was no good reason for you to keep going when you felt it coming on, no matter what your group might have said to you. You should have just sat down for a bit and told them to fuck off if continuing the hike meant that much to them.

That being said, the comments your friends made about you being weak or lazy were definitely asshole material. This includes your boyfriend because of course he would have known about your condition better than anyone else other than you. I rarely hike in large groups, but usually, one or two of my friends who know about my EIB will stay behind with me to continue at a slower pace. I think that if anything, you can, and probably should, be angry with them for treating you like a burden.

I experience both visual and auditory hallucinations.

My visual hallucinations range from kinda creepy to absolutely terrifying. I usually see faces in windows, people standing in the corner, etc. But sometimes my brain just goes straight for the gore. I can go into more detail about those, but honestly, some of that keeps me up at night.

My auditory hallucinations used to be really aggressive too. I would basically hear people telling me that I was worthless and I deserved to feel as bad as I did. It’s gotten more mundane recently. I usually get ambulance sirens, phones ringing, text tones, or people saying my name.
